Summary: The paper compares generation strategies for writing OMIM-style phenotype entries from exactly the papers the curators cited, holding the model (Claude Opus 5.5), the supplied sources, the guards, a claim-level audit and the scoring fixed. The benchmark uses 100 OMIM phenotype entries with 2-12 references (515 papers, 19% readable in full via open access). The primary endpoint, 'OMIM facts conveyed', scores what a draft says about each cited paper against 6,652 atomic facts split once from OMIM's allelic-variant paragraphs as deposited in ClinVar; secondary measures cover HPO synopsis terms, variants, causal gene and inheritance. Strategies span read-and-write (direct reading, an agentic curator), extract-then-write (evidence graph, case table), memory-first (recall then verify), a memory-only control and three add-ons. Main findings: hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% on 46 entries (+43.7 points, 95% CI 38.3-49.1); the agent and evidence graph are within about 0.5 points of direct reading and the case table trails by 1.9 (CI -3.1 to -0.8), with orderings that depend on entry set and settings (matched ablation, App. F); on 38 held-out entries a completeness pass adds 2.6 points while lengthening drafts by about a third; and a planted-error study shows the audit catches citation swaps and single-value substitutions but cannot see added citations (best-verdict rule) or omissions. All judgements are made by the writer's model family and none was validated by a person. The paper has extensive appendices on completion, safety-filter stops, replicates, post hoc status of analyses, released pipelines (PaperQA2, GraphRAG, STORM), input padding and cost.
Strengths: Careful controlled design: one model, the curators' own reference lists, shared guards, one audit and one scoring procedure, so differences can be attributed to the strategy (Sec. 3, Fig. 1). The within-paper access manipulation (same entries, full text hidden vs shown; Sec. 4.1, Table 24) is a clean way to separate access from paper selection, unlike the observational per-access breakdown that the authors correctly flag as confounded (Table 13).

Unusually transparent reporting. Every experiment's status (pre-specified / post hoc / exploratory), entry set and attrition is tabulated (Tables 2-3); post hoc choices (a)-(i) are listed explicitly (Sec. 3.3); a corrected earlier analysis is disclosed (App. M.4); and completion under safety-filter stops is treated as an outcome with a symmetric comparison rule and an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Table 11).

Fixed fact lists split once without sight of any draft, paired bootstrap intervals with sign tests and Holm adjustment for secondary measures, plus judge-variation and run-to-run replicates (App. E, Table 20) used as a yardstick (1.0-point half-width over 93 entries). This is much more rigorous than typical LLM-system comparisons.

The decomposition of coverage by whether the supplied text states a fact (Fig. 2b-c, Table 19) is informative: reading strategies convey 91-94% of stated facts and about 6% of unstated ones, no better than the memory-only control on the latter, which locates where the remaining headroom is (about 4% of facts; Sec. 4.1).

The audit blind-spot analysis (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 4, App. L) is useful to practitioners: it shows concretely that a best-verdict-over-cited-papers rule cannot detect over-citation (0/30 added citations flagged although the added paper's own verdict was 'unsupported' for all 176 claims) and that omissions are invisible by construction, and quantifies weak sensitivity to deleted qualifiers (11/30).

Practical reporting of cost, calls, tokens and draft length beside quality (Tables 12, 34), and a memory-only control by creation era including entries created after model development (Fig. 5, App. M.2) to address contamination.
Weaknesses: The headline access result is largely implied by how the reference is constructed. The reference consists of variant-centred paragraphs that curators wrote from full papers; the supplied text states 76% of facts about full-text papers but only 26% about abstract-only papers (Fig. 2b, Table 19), and reading strategies convey over 90% of stated facts (Fig. 2c). The 79.8% vs 36.1% contrast therefore largely re-measures how much of the reference is present in abstracts, which the paper itself calls 'expected' (Sec. 1, l.91). It is useful to have the size measured for biocuration, but it is not a surprising finding.

The strategy comparison is run in a near-ceiling regime that has little power to separate designs. Entries have 2-12 references and fit one prompt, 81% of papers are abstracts or titles, and only about 4% of facts are 'not fully conveyed although stated' (Sec. 4.1, l.320-322), so differences between designs are bounded to a few points by construction. The paper says so (Sec. 5, l.505), but the regimes where agents or intermediate representations are expected to help could not be evaluated: no large entry was completed by every strategy (App. K.2), the 30-75-reference tier yields no findings (App. M.1), and the padding test used unrelated papers that every strategy ignored, testing input size rather than crowding (App. K.1). The conclusion that 'designs differ by a few points either way' therefore holds for the easiest regime only.

Measurement validity rests entirely on unvalidated judgements by the writer's own model family: fact splitting, coverage marks, the 'stated' classification, and the audit (Sec. 3.3; Limitation (i)). The 95.7% agreement between two judgings (App. E) shows only self-consistency. The 43.7-point access effect is too large to be a judge artifact, but the strategy differences of 0.5-2 points are well within what self-preference or style bias could produce, especially since extract-then-write drafts are systematically longer (113.5 and 117.9 vs 101.0 audited claims; Table 1). For a benchmark paper, a stratified expert-labelled sample with chance-corrected agreement, or at least a judge from another model family, is a major missing piece.

The primary endpoint measures recall only and does not control for length. The completeness pass adds 2.6 points while drafts grow from 10,802 to 14,412 characters (Sec. 4.3); the three-draft merge adds 3.1 points but lowers fidelity (95.8% supported, variant precision 83.4% vs 87.1%; Tables 33-34). Only about 24% of a direct-reading draft's statements have a counterpart in the reference (App. H), so most draft content is outside the primary endpoint. The only precision-side check for the reading-better arms is the audited share supported on 20 entries with no interval (Table 33). Without a length-normalised or precision-paired endpoint, part of the reading-better gains may come simply from writing more.

Benchmark reusability is limited. The curator text and fixed fact lists are not redistributed (Sec. 3.1 'Reuse'; Ethics statement), so scoring a new strategy needs a rebuilt and re-split reference, whose stability under a fresh split by the same procedure was not measured. Splitting afresh per draft ran 2-5 points higher (Table 6). That undercuts contribution (1): the motivation is comparisons with sources and scoring held fixed, yet outside groups cannot score on the same denominators.

Results are tied to one proprietary model, whose safety filter caused uneven, opaque attrition: 7 of 100 main entries excluded (Table 5); 10 of 30 entries created in 2026 lost (App. M.2); no large entry compared (App. K.2); STORM produced no article (App. J). The reading-better gains depend on the fallback rule: counting a stopped revision as zero turns +2.4 and +3.1 into -3.5 and -4.8 on the mean (Table 32; Sec. 4.3). The authors acknowledge this, but it means the ordering of strategies and the size of the gains may not transfer to other writers, including smaller-context models (Limitation (ii)).

Several reported effects rest on choices made after results were seen. The symmetric completion rule was adopted after a first analysis placed the evidence graph 2.1 points below direct reading (Sec. 3.3(b), App. M.4). The fixed fact lists replaced per-draft splitting (3.3(a)). The case table's clearest deficit (-8.4 on stated full-text facts) comes from a post hoc restriction (Fig. 3a, Table 19). The fourth reading-better arm was designed after the others' held-out results were seen. The labelling is honest, but without a pre-registered protocol the main comparison carries less evidential weight than its intervals suggest.

Memorisation is not excluded as a contributor to the reading results. The causal gene is 'withheld', yet memory alone names it with F1 88.9-100% in the four older bands (Table 16). Direct reading's coverage of abstract-only facts declines with creation era from 49.8% to 37.9% (Table 15; Fig. 5 caption), a pattern consistent with memory helping older entries, which the paper notes but 'did not analyse' (Sec. 4.2, l.373-376). The clean held-out test is 20 entries (App. M.2).

Paradigm-level conclusions rest on one implementation per paradigm (Limitation (iii)), and the ablation shows implementation settings moving the case table by +2.1 points (Table 21), comparable to the between-design differences. The released-pipeline comparisons are on 10 and 4 entries, with PaperQA2 run without its agent and STORM producing nothing (App. J). These do not support claims about the designs as such, and the paper partly acknowledges this.

Presentation is very dense and hard to follow. The main text packs about ten experiments into ten pages, with heavy hedging and nested parenthetical qualifiers (e.g., the abstract and the paragraphs of Sec. 4.2). Central terms ('symmetric rule', 'like for like', 'stated', 'held out') are defined in one compressed paragraph (Sec. 3.3), and much of the substance is in about 40 pages of appendices with more than 50 tables. The core story (access effect; strategy parity; audit blind spots) competes with add-ons, released systems, padding, updates and retrieval. The title is long and does not state the finding. Focusing the main text and moving secondary threads out would make the contribution much clearer.

Fit and significance for ICLR are modest. No new method is proposed, and the insights are mainly domain-specific to biocuration under open-access constraints, for a single model. The paper reads more like a careful evaluation report for a bioinformatics or datasets-and-benchmarks venue than a contribution of general interest to representation-learning research.
Questions: In the hidden-full-text experiment (Sec. 4.1, Table 24), are the 2,120 facts in 136 paragraphs restricted to paragraphs about the hidden full-text papers, or do they include paragraphs about abstract-only papers in the same 46 entries? If mixed, please report the contrast on hidden-paper facts only.

Can you add any human validation, even 150-300 facts stratified by strategy and access level, for the coverage judge and the 'stated' judge, with Cohen's kappa against a curator or domain expert? Would the 0.5-2-point strategy differences survive the observed disagreement rate?
Would a judge from a different model family reproduce the ordering of strategies and the sign of the case-table deficit on the 93 entries, or at least on the 30-entry replicate subset?

Please report a length-controlled view of the reading-better arms, for example coverage per 1,000 characters, or coverage after truncating each draft to the baseline's length per paper, so the gain from reading more completely can be separated from the gain from writing more.

How stable are levels and paired differences under an independent second split of the same curator paragraphs by the same procedure? Two splits on a subset would show whether results reported 'within one split' transfer to a rebuilt reference.
Could you release, for reuse, the splitting prompt with per-fact identifiers and hashes of the fact text, so that groups with licensed access can verify they reconstructed the same denominators?

For the case table's 130 variants not listed by OMIM (Table 10), how many are actually reported in the cited papers? The current precision definition counts these as misses whether or not the paper reports them, which may penalise thorough extraction.

The decline of direct reading's abstract-only coverage with creation era (Table 15) is attributed to neither memory nor composition. Can you test it, for example by comparing coverage on facts the memory-only draft also conveys versus facts it does not, by band?

Since safety-filter stops are frequent and uneven, did you consider a pre-specified sensitivity analysis with a neutral rewording or a second model for stopped calls only, to check whether the attrition biases the comparison?
Limitations: The authors' limitations section (Sec. 5, (i)-(xii)) is thorough and candid; the main ones are no human validation and a single model family for writing, auditing and judging.

The regime (2-12 references, papers fitting one prompt, mostly abstracts) is the one most favourable to direct reading; results may not extend to entries with many relevant papers, where designs could separate.
The primary endpoint is recall-only with no length or precision counterpart, and covers only about a quarter of what drafts say.
The reference cannot be redistributed, so others cannot reproduce the scoring denominators, and fresh-split stability is unmeasured.
Safety-filter attrition specific to one model affects completion, the large-entry tiers, a released pipeline (STORM), and the size of reading-better gains (Table 32).
Possible memorisation of public OMIM content is not ruled out for older entries; the held-out 2026 check covers 20 entries.
The audit checks fidelity to the cited text, not correctness or completeness, and is blind to over-citation; the planted-error study is small (30 items per class) and exploratory.
